title: Batch 8 Gospels / Historical Jesus Geography Curation Methodology
notes: Separates Gospel textual geography, independently attested first-century history, archaeological sites, later pilgrimage traditions, and competing identifications. Uncertain Passion and ministry locations are left unpinned rather than forced onto a modern coordinate.

title: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John — canonical geographic sequence
notes: Batch 8 stores references and project-authored summaries, not full verse text. Synoptic and Johannine geography are not harmonized beyond what the texts explicitly support.

title: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, Book 17
author: Flavius Josephus
notes: Primary literary source for Herod the Great’s final years, succession, Archelaus, and related political chronology.

title: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, Book 18
author: Flavius Josephus
notes: Primary literary source for Quirinius, Roman prefects, Herod Antipas, John the Baptist, Pilate, and Caiaphas-era context. It is not treated as an archaeological source.

title: Josephus, Jewish War, Book 1
author: Flavius Josephus
notes: Source for Herodian building, fortresses, and political history.

title: Josephus, Jewish War, Book 2
author: Flavius Josephus
notes: Source for Herodian succession, Roman administration, Jerusalem, and provincial context.

title: Philo, Embassy to Gaius (Legatio ad Gaium)
author: Philo of Alexandria
notes: Ancient literary evidence for Pilate and the use of Herod’s palace in Jerusalem in the episode of the gilded shields; relevant to praetorium debates.

title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44
author: Tacitus
notes: Roman literary reference to Christus being executed under Pontius Pilate during Tiberius’s reign. Later than the events and used as independent Roman literary context.

title: Pontius Pilate inscription from Caesarea Maritima
notes: Inscription naming Pontius Pilate and his prefectural office. It anchors Pilate historically at Caesarea; it does not identify the Jerusalem trial location.

title: “Joseph son of Caiaphas” ossuary and Jerusalem burial context
notes: An ornate ossuary bearing the name Yosef bar Qayafa is often associated with the high-priestly Caiaphas family. The personal identification is plausible but should not be treated as absolutely certain.

title: Early Roman Nazareth archaeological synthesis
notes: Represents published archaeological work on early Roman settlement, domestic architecture, agricultural installations, and tombs at Nazareth. Used only to establish settlement context, not specific Gospel houses.

title: Sepphoris / Zippori archaeological publications
notes: Used for urban context in Lower Galilee and Antipas-era development; no Gospel visit is inferred.

title: Cana of Galilee identification research — Khirbet Qana and Kafr Kanna traditions
notes: Used to preserve the distinction between the unlocated Gospel village, archaeological candidate Khirbet Qana, and later Kafr Kanna pilgrimage tradition.

title: Capernaum archaeological publications
notes: Used for Roman-period village occupation, domestic remains, synagogue sequence, and settlement context. “House of Peter” identification is not treated as certain.

title: Bethsaida identification research — el-Araj and et-Tell
notes: Represents the continuing archaeological debate over Bethsaida/Julias. Both major candidates are kept distinct and neither is promoted to established Gospel identification.

title: Archaeology of Roman Galilee — regional synthesis
notes: Used for settlement, economy, roads, synagogues, and urban-rural context in first-century Galilee.

title: Magdala / Migdal early Roman archaeological publications
notes: Used for the early Roman synagogue, harbor-related remains, ritual baths, and settlement context.

title: Critical New Testament geography — Galilee, Decapolis, and Gospel place-name problems
notes: Used for textual variants and disputed identifications such as Gerasenes/Gadarenes/Gergesenes and Aenon near Salim.

title: New Testament Samaria and Sychar geographic studies
notes: Used for Sychar, Askar, Shechem, Jacob’s Well tradition, and Mount Gerizim context; no single Sychar identification is treated as established.

title: Bethany beyond the Jordan / baptism-site archaeological and textual research
notes: Used to distinguish the unlocated Johannine Bethany from the early Christian baptismal landscape at al-Maghtas/Wadi al-Kharrar.

title: Machaerus archaeological publications
notes: Used for the established Herodian fortress at Mukawir. The connection to John the Baptist derives especially from Josephus, not from an excavated labeled prison cell.

title: Second Temple Jerusalem archaeological and topographic synthesis
notes: Used for Temple Mount environs, Herodian western palace, pools, walls, Kidron/Mount of Olives geography, and Passion topography. Specific Gospel rooms and trial stations remain uncertain.

title: Pilate’s Jerusalem praetorium — western palace and Antonia debate
notes: Used to keep candidate locations distinct. The project does not equate the later Via Dolorosa route with a recovered first-century Passion itinerary.

title: Bethesda and Siloam archaeological publications
notes: Used for the excavated pool complexes and their Second Temple-period phases.

title: Church of the Holy Sepulchre — archaeology and historical topography
notes: Used for quarry/tomb archaeology, ancient Christian tradition, and the site’s relationship to reconstructed first-century city walls. Compatibility is not presented as proof of the crucifixion or burial.

title: Garden Tomb archaeological assessment
notes: Used to explain the modern tradition and the commonly accepted earlier dating of the rock-cut tomb, which weighs against identifying it as a newly cut first-century tomb.

title: Emmaus identification research — distance variants and candidate sites
notes: Used to preserve Luke 24 manuscript-distance issues and multiple candidates without selecting one as certain.

title: Transfiguration mountain geographic traditions and proposals
notes: Used to separate Mount Tabor tradition from Mount Hermon and other modern proposals; the Gospel mountain remains unnamed.
